name: Colloidal silver
lead: Colloidal silver is a suspension of tiny silver particles in a liquid, historically described as nanosilver when the particles are below 100 nanometres. It is promoted in some alternative-health circles as a dietary supplement to ingest as a health or immune aid [1][2]. Wikipedia says colloidal silver has been marketed as an essential mineral supplement and as a way to prevent or treat cancer, diabetes, arthritis, HIV/AIDS, herpes and tuberculosis, and states that no medical evidence supports it for these claims [1].

The best-documented appearance-related effect is argyria, a blue-grey discolouration of skin and other tissues that Wikipedia says can follow chronic ingestion or inhalation of silver, including colloidal silver, and that does not resolve after exposure stops [4].

Silver in dressings and sinus irrigations has been investigated in laboratory and clinical settings, and reviews state that nanosilver is not inert in the body [2][5][6]. No study found has examined ingested colloidal silver for appearance.
infobox: Evidence for health or appearance claims

paras: Wikipedia describes silver nanoparticles as particles between 1 and 100 nm, many of which are used as a colloid, and says that M. C. Lea made a citrate-stabilised silver colloid in 1889. Promotion of colloidal silver as a dietary supplement resumed around 1990 [1]. A 2011 analysis found that colloidal silver had been used for more than 100 years and registered as a biocidal material in the United States since 1954 [7].

Wikipedia reports claims that colloidal silver can prevent or treat conditions including cancer, diabetes, arthritis, HIV/AIDS, herpes and tuberculosis, and states that silver is not an essential mineral for humans [1]. A 2015 review notes that colloidal silver is considered by many to be an ideal agent against pathogens without the side effects of antibiotics, but that toxicological research indicates nanosilver is not inert in the body [2].

Wikipedia says ingested silver, including colloidal silver, can cause argyria, and that the condition is cosmetically undesirable and not life-threatening, although research on possible kidney and night-vision effects is not definitive [1][4]. It also states argyria worsens with continued exposure and persists after exposure ends because silver cannot be removed from tissue [4].

Wikipedia cites two publicised cases. Stan Jones, a US Senate candidate in 2002 and 2006, said he took colloidal silver as a precaution against antibiotic shortages during Y2K, and Paul Karason was described in 2007 press reports as turning blue after taking a homemade silver colloid and applying silver salve [4]. Earlier descriptions of grey or blue-grey discolouration from silver appear in medical publications from 1843 and 1859 [4].

A 2015 occupational review reported that inhaled silver nanoparticles had adverse effects mainly on the liver and lungs of rats, via oxidative stress [2], and a 2014 review examined oral toxicity of silver ions, nanoparticles and colloidal silver [8]. The US EPA classifies silver nanoparticles used for antimicrobial purposes as pesticides [1].

No studies found on ingesting colloidal silver for appearance. Human studies of silver products for other purposes include a controlled study in which an orally taken commercial colloidal silver product produced detectable serum silver after 14 days but no clinically significant changes in metabolic, blood, urinary or physical findings or in cytochrome P450 enzyme activity [6]. A placebo-controlled study examined commercial silver nanoparticles and ex vivo platelet aggregation [9]. Randomised trials have examined topical colloidal silver in recalcitrant chronic rhinosinusitis and a colloidal silver device for upper airway disease in children [10][11], and reviews describe colloidal silver irrigation as a novel treatment under investigation for sinus infection whose evidence base is limited [5][12].

Discussion of colloidal silver in appearance-focused communities is small compared with other fringe practices; its connection to the topic is mainly through health claims and the visible effect of argyria. No forum material was reviewed for this article.

timeline.event: Medical publications describe silver causing grey or blue-grey skin, per Wikipedia [4].

lore.intro: Claims about colloidal silver circulate in alternative-health communities; no looksmaxxing forum material was available for this entry, so the claims below reflect marketed claims reported by Wikipedia [1].

claims.claim: Ingesting colloidal silver treats or prevents illness
claims.believers: Promoters market it as an immune or antimicrobial supplement for conditions ranging from infections to cancer [1].
claims.experts: Wikipedia states no medical evidence supports colloidal silver for any claimed use and that silver is not an essential mineral [1].

claims.claim: Colloidal silver has no side effects
claims.believers: Some advocates consider it an ideal antimicrobial agent without the side effects of antibiotics [2].
claims.experts: A review says nanosilver is not inert in the body, and Wikipedia reports that chronic ingestion can cause permanent argyria [2][4].

card.summary: Ingested silver suspension sold as a health supplement; claims are unsupported per Wikipedia and chronic use can cause permanent blue-grey skin (argyria).
card.note: Argyria is described as permanent once it develops.

quick.overview:
Colloidal silver is a suspension of very small silver particles that some alternative-health sources promote as a supplement to ingest for immunity and illness. It has a long history as an antimicrobial and was registered as a biocide in the US in 1954.

Wikipedia states no medical evidence supports it for the claimed uses, and silver is not an essential mineral. Its most visible documented effect on appearance is argyria, a lasting blue-grey skin colour.
quick.mechanism: Silver particles have antimicrobial properties in laboratory and wound-dressing contexts, and are used in medical devices and textiles. Reviews say ingested nanosilver is not inert and distributes to tissues such as the liver.
quick.risks: Chronic ingestion or inhalation of silver can cause argyria, which Wikipedia says does not resolve after exposure stops. Reviews report liver and lung effects of inhaled nanosilver in rats, and the US EPA classifies antimicrobial silver nanoparticles as pesticides.
